Triggers.value: Night-time or waking up in the dark

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs

vignette:
Alex, a 33-year-old graphic designer, traces the collapse of his life back to a single evening nine months ago. He and his then-wife had been walking home from a late dinner when an unmarked dark sedan screeched to a halt beside them. Two men in plainclothes, later identified as police officers, burst out, shouting commands he couldn't process. Before he could react, he was slammed against a brick wall, the rough texture scraping his cheek. The incident was a brutal case of mistaken identity, lasting only a few minutes before panicked apologies were made, but the damage was already done. The memory of the blinding headlights pinning him, the feeling of being trapped and powerless in the sudden, violent crowd of two bodies pressing him into the wall, and the overwhelming darkness surrounding the scene became the architecture of his new reality.

In the months that followed, Alex’s world began to shrink. The triggers were everywhere, ambushing him in the most mundane moments of his day. A car similar to the officers’—any dark, heavy sedan—would cause a surge of panic so intense he’d have to duck into a doorway, his heart hammering against his ribs. To manage this, he began keeping a flask of whiskey in his work bag, taking a sharp swallow to quell the shaking in his hands after such an encounter. This practice escalated; what started as a reactive measure soon became a preemptive one, with him drinking before even leaving the house for a client meeting. He eventually lost his in-office position and transitioned to freelance work, unable to handle the daily commute and the unpredictability of the city streets.

Crowded places became unbearable territories. A trip to the grocery store or a walk through a busy downtown plaza would evoke the same feeling of being pinned and suffocated he’d felt against that wall. When caught in a crowd, his first, almost involuntary reaction was to cover his face with his hands, a protective gesture that did little to stop the rising tide of fear but drew confused and concerned stares from strangers. This shame only compounded his isolation. He found himself avoiding any situation that might involve a queue or a crowd, which meant no more concerts, no more farmers' markets, and eventually, no more dinners out with his wife. Similarly, the sight of a police or even a private security uniform would send him into a state of high alert, forcing him to abruptly change his route or abandon his errands for the day.

The most relentless trigger, however, was the dark. Alex developed a profound fear of nighttime, a condition that made sleep a nightly battle. He would often jolt awake in the pitch-black of his bedroom, disoriented and convinced he was back on that sidewalk. In those moments of terror, his only recourse was the cocktail of sleeping pills and alcohol he kept on his nightstand. The immediate, dulling effect was the only thing that could silence the replay of events in his mind and allow him to drift back into a troubled sleep. This nightly ritual became a dangerous dependency, a maladaptive solution that only deepened the chasm between him and his wife, who saw him becoming a ghost in his own home. His divorce was finalized two months ago. It was this final, devastating loss that prompted him to seek help, leaving him with the desperate hope of one day being able to simply exist in the world again without being hunted by his own mind.
